subject: biology
timingNote: Higher Level: 2h 30m, 300 marks (60% of your grade; the Biology in Practice Investigation is the other 40%, 200 marks). Seven questions of 50 marks each: Question 1 is compulsory and you answer any five of Questions 2 to 7. This is the new Biology course, and this guide is based on the SEC's four published sample papers (two Higher Level, two Ordinary Level). The SEC did not publish marking schemes for them, so mark splits below are marked as estimates where they are not stated.

examDay.task: The 2027 start time for Biology was not confirmed when this was written, so the timeline starts at 9:30 as an example. You get one answer booklet (the questions are printed in it and you write in the spaces, on the graphs and on the diagrams provided), with spare writing pages and graph paper at the back. Answer in blue or black pen, pencil only for sketches, graphs and diagrams. The booklet is scanned and marked on screen.
facts: Question 1 is compulsory. Then answer any five of Questions 2 to 7. All seven carry 50 marks. Only five of the six optional questions count, so you drop one question completely.
First exam on the new course

2027 is the first year Biology is examined on the new specification. The old Section A, B and C paper is gone: there are no sections and no experiment questions chosen from a list. The only mark guides are the SEC sample papers, so treat them as the blueprint.

The written paper is 300 marks (60%). The Biology in Practice Investigation is 200 marks (40%), completed in school and marked by the SEC. Nothing you do in the exam hall changes the investigation mark.

Same shape: 2h 30m, 300 marks, Question 1 compulsory plus five of Questions 2 to 7. Questions give more support: tick boxes, matching, completed tables, some steps already filled in, and shorter 'identify' and 'state' parts. Question 1 includes scientific inquiry (experimental design, presenting results).

timeline.label: Choose
timeline.detail: Skim Questions 2 to 7 and pick your five. You are choosing which question to drop.

timeline.label: Question 1
timeline.detail: Compulsory: 5 or 6 short parts across the whole course, so 25 minutes and no more.

timeline.label: Question 2
timeline.detail: Roughly half a minute per mark. Stop when the 24 minutes are up.

timeline.label: Question 3
timeline.detail: Same pace. Graphs and diagrams eat time, so start them with 6 minutes left in the question.

timeline.label: Question 4
timeline.detail: Same pace. Short parts first, longer descriptions last.

timeline.label: Question 5
timeline.detail: Same pace. Never leave a part blank: wrong answers lose nothing.

timeline.label: Question 6
timeline.detail: Last question. If you finish early, go back to graphs and diagrams you skipped.

tips.timing: About 25 minutes for 50 marks. Question 1 is the only one you cannot skip, so do not spend extra time on a part you find hard: it is spread over lots of small items from different topics.
tips.structure: In the Higher Level samples Question 1 has 5 or 6 parts, (a) to (e) or (f), each on a different topic (digestion, nervous system, a plant experiment, hormones, kidney, fungi in Sample 1; cell cycle, a vaccine trial, cell membrane, plant tissue, prions in Sample 2). Each part is 3 to 4 short items: name it, state it, mark it on a diagram, read a graph. Practice questions here come from the old course (the old Section A short questions), which has the same short-answer style.
reminders: Because every part is a different topic, you cannot revise just a few chapters and rely on Question 1: it tests the whole course
Write inside the answer spaces, on the graph or on the diagram. Anything outside them may not be seen, because the booklet is scanned
Include units when a number has them: the paper warns you can lose marks without them
Show working or supporting work when asked to explain or calculate: the paper warns you may lose marks without it
Use pencil only for sketches, graphs and diagrams; everything else is blue or black pen

questionTypes.name: Identify, name and state
questionTypes.where: Every part of Question 1, in both Sample 1 and Sample 2. Examples: identify organs A and B of the digestive system, name the parts of a nephron, name the tissues X, Y and Z in a plant stem, state a function of tissue Y.
questionTypes.see: A labelled image or short sentence followed by 'identify', 'name', 'state' or 'what is meant by'. Example, Sample 1 Q1(e)(iii): 'Name a constituent of the blood not normally present in urine.'
questionTypes.marked: The SEC did not publish a marking scheme for the sample papers, so the mark per item is not confirmed. With about 18 items in a 50-mark question, most items are worth about 2 to 3 marks. Name only what is asked: one correct answer scores, and extra wrong answers can undo it.
questionTypes.play: Answer in 3 to 10 words, straight from the course vocabulary. If a word is asked for, write the word, not a sentence. Do not leave any box empty.
traps: Giving two answers when one is asked, where one of them is wrong
Writing a description when a one-word name is asked for
Using everyday words (tube, flap, bit) instead of the biological term

questionTypes.name: Mark it on the diagram
questionTypes.where: Question 1 in both Higher Level samples. Examples: draw an arrow to show the direction of the nerve impulse; write F where ultrafiltration happens on the nephron; write X on a cell membrane in a micrograph; draw an arrow from label X to the bacteria on an image.
questionTypes.see: An existing diagram or photo with an instruction to add a letter or arrow. Example, Sample 1 Q1(b)(ii): 'On the diagram, draw an arrow to show the direction the nerve impulse is transferred.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published for the samples. These are position answers: the mark depends on where the arrow or letter lands, so a vague mark or a mark between two structures is likely to be treated as wrong.
questionTypes.play: Place the letter or arrowhead clearly on the exact structure. Use pencil if you are unsure so you can rub it out cleanly. Write the exact letter asked for (X, Y, F).
traps: Arrows that point between two structures
Writing the letter in the margin instead of on the structure
Writing the answer in the text box when the question says 'on the diagram'

questionTypes.name: Read the graph or table
questionTypes.where: Question 1 in both Higher Level samples. Examples: a table of cucumber mass change in different salt concentrations; a blood glucose graph where you mark X for insulin and Y for glucagon.
questionTypes.see: A short data table or graph, then a conclusion or a mark-the-time question. Example, Sample 1 Q1(c)(iii): 'What conclusion can the student make from this investigation based on the data collected?'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published. The conclusion items ask you to link the independent variable to the result, so a bare restatement of the numbers is unlikely to be enough.
questionTypes.play: Say what changes as the independent variable increases, and use the figures: 'As salt concentration rises, the mass change falls from +0.5 g to -0.5 g.' For a mark-the-time question, think of the cause: insulin starts to rise after glucose rises, not before.
traps: Stating the independent variable but not the effect on the result
Writing the conclusion without a direction ('mass changes')
Marking X or Y at the peak or trough when the question asks when secretion starts to increase

questionTypes.name: Labelled diagram from memory
questionTypes.where: Question 1(f) in Sample 1 (draw a labelled diagram of Rhizopus). Also Question 4(a)(ii) in Sample 2 (labelled bacterial cell).
questionTypes.see: A blank box and an instruction. Example, Sample 1 Q1(f)(ii): 'Draw a labelled diagram of Rhizopus.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published for the samples. In the old course a diagram was marked as 6 for the diagram, plus 3 for labels (3 marks for any three correct labels), with the diagram graded 6, 3 or 0. Expect the same style: one mark for a correct label only counts if the part is in the right place.
questionTypes.play: Learn one diagram per living group by heart (fungus: hypha, sporangium, spores, rhizoid, stolon). Draw big, in pencil, then label with straight lines that touch the structure.
traps: A small, cramped diagram where label lines cross
Labels that say 'cell' or 'part' instead of the structure name
Leaving out one key part: the old scheme scored a diagram 3 if one part was missing

questionTypes.name: Suggest or explain
questionTypes.where: Question 1(e)(iv) Sample 1 (why is part B longer in camels?). Question 1(b) and (e) in Sample 2 (why test a vaccine worldwide, why prions are pathogens, why folding matters).
questionTypes.see: Questions that start with 'suggest', 'explain' or 'justify' and have lines or a box. Example, Sample 2 Q1(b)(iv): 'Would it be correct to conclude that this vaccine works in children under the age of 16 years? Justify your answer.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published. Justify and explain items are worth more than name items: you need a claim and a reason. A yes or no on its own is not enough.
questionTypes.play: Give the answer, then 'because', then the fact from the stimulus. 'No, because the trial only included people aged 16 or over, so there is no data for children.'
traps: Giving the answer without the reason
Repeating the question in different words
Ignoring the information in the passage: these questions are set on it

sections.name: Questions 2 to 7 – Structured Questions (answer any five)

tips.timing: About 24 minutes per question, 120 minutes for the five. That is under half a minute per mark. Do not stay on one part: every question is built from 3 or 4 lettered parts, and the last item of a part is usually the hardest.
tips.structure: Each question is 50 marks with parts (a) to (c) or (d), and each part has between 3 and 7 items. Each question mixes topics: Sample 1 Question 2 is enzymes, fermentation, classification and a data graph. Sample 2 Question 2 is diversity, nitrogen cycle and a flower diagram. Practice questions here come from the old course: the old experiment questions (Section B) and long questions (Section C) are the closest match for the longer descriptions and the experiment parts.
reminders: Pick the five questions where you can do the graphs and calculations: those are the marks other students lose
Most parts open with a passage, diagram or data set. Read it first, because the question items are set on it
Command words matter: 'state' and 'name' need a few words; 'describe', 'explain', 'outline' and 'discuss' need developed answers
Plot graphs in the space or on the spare graph paper at the back, labelled with the question number and part
Do not leave blanks: there is no negative marking

questionTypes.name: Passage or data stimulus, then apply
questionTypes.where: Every question from 2 to 7 in all four sample papers. Examples: grove snail shell colours and the song thrush food chain (Sample 1 Q4); Venus flytrap in a bog (Sample 2 Q6); Rhododendron invading woodland (Sample 1 Q7).
questionTypes.see: A short passage, usually adapted from a real source, then items that ask you to apply the course to it. Example, Sample 1 Q4(b)(ii): 'The population of song thrushes has declined steeply over the last fifty years. Suggest one possible explanation for this decline.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published for the samples. Application items such as 'suggest' are likely to accept any biologically sound idea, so answers that use the passage and the course earn more than copied text.
questionTypes.play: Underline two or three key facts in the passage first. Answer using one of those facts plus one course idea.
traps: Copying a sentence from the passage as the whole answer
Suggesting something unrelated to the organism in the passage
Writing a general fact about the topic when the item asks about this example

questionTypes.name: Plot or draw a graph
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q3(c)(iii) (blood pH of two people over 30 minutes), Q7(b)(i) (CO2 from invaded and native soil, over nine months), and Sample 2 Q6 (light intensity results as a line graph). Also 'draw a line to predict' items (fermentation at 4 °C, Sample 1 Q2(d)(ii)).
questionTypes.marks: about 5 to 8 marks for a full graph (estimate)
questionTypes.see: A data table and a blank grid. Example, Sample 1 Q3(c)(iii): 'On the grid below, plot a suitable graph to represent all the data in the table above.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published. The wording 'all the data' means both people or both soils must be on the same grid, and a graph generally needs labelled axes with units, a suitable scale, correct points and a key. Old-course schemes also gave marks separately for axes, plotting and joining the points.
questionTypes.play: Choose a line graph for time series. Use more than half the grid. Label both axes with the quantity and unit. Plot every point with a small cross, join them with a ruler or smooth line, and add a key if there are two lines.
traps: Only plotting one of the two data sets
Axes without units or labels
Uneven scale on the time axis
For a prediction line, drawing it but not showing the direction of the change

questionTypes.name: Calculate
questionTypes.where: Sample 2 Q2(a)(iii) (species diversity index from six species counts, with the formula given), Sample 2 Q5 (heart rate from a graph), Sample 1 Q4(a) (genotypes and gametes, a cross), Sample 1 Q6(d) (DNA to mRNA, amino acids, number of DNA fragments).
questionTypes.see: A data table or sequence, a formula (when needed) and a box. Example, Sample 2 Q2(a)(iii): 'Using the data and formula, calculate the species diversity index for County Cork.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published. The paper warns: 'You may lose marks if your solutions do not include relevant supporting work' and 'if the appropriate units of measurement are not included'. Working earns marks even if the final number is wrong.
questionTypes.play: Write the formula, substitute each number, then give the answer to a sensible number of decimal places with units. For a cross, draw a Punnett square for the gametes and list each genotype and phenotype.
traps: Writing only the final number with no working
Leaving out units (beats per minute, mm, mg/L)
Mixing up N and n in the diversity index formula
Writing the wrong strand: mRNA has U instead of T

questionTypes.name: Draw or model a diagram
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q4(b)(i) (draw a pyramid of biomass from a food chain), Sample 2 Q2(c)(iii) (labelled diagram of the structure of a flower), Sample 2 Q4(a)(ii) (labelled bacterial cell), Sample 2 Q5 (model a structural difference between an artery and a vein).
questionTypes.see: A box and the verbs 'draw', 'model' or 'sketch'. Example, Sample 1 Q4(b)(i): 'Using organisms from the article above, model a food chain and draw a pyramid of biomass of this food chain.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published for the samples. 'Model' means the diagram itself is the answer: it must show the idea, not just the names. In the old course, diagrams were graded (6, 3 or 0), with extra marks for labels, so unlabelled diagrams lose a share.
questionTypes.play: Build the food chain from the passage in order (producer to top predator), then draw the pyramid with the producer widest at the bottom and each level narrower. Label each bar with the organism name. Draw large, label with ruled lines.
traps: Using organisms that are not in the passage
Wrong order in the food chain or the pyramid
Labels without lines to the structure, or a drawing too small to label
Drawing an artery and a vein but not showing the difference the question asks for (wall thickness, lumen, valves)

questionTypes.name: Describe or explain a process
questionTypes.where: Sample 1: zygote development to implantation (Q5(c)(i)), DNA fragment separation (Q6(d)(iv)), thylakoid electron pathways (Q7(d)). Sample 2: non-cyclic pathway of the light-dependent reactions (Q6(c)), nitrogen fixation (Q2(b)(v)), gel electrophoresis (Q3(b)(ii)), how enzymes catalyse reactions (Q7).
questionTypes.see: A single item with 'describe', 'outline' or 'explain', often with lines under it. Example, Sample 2 Q6(c): 'Describe the non-cyclic pathway of the light dependent reactions of photosynthesis.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published for the samples. Process answers are marked in the old course by points: one mark per correct distinct point, so every sentence needs to carry a fact. Saying the same thing in two ways scores once.
questionTypes.play: Put it in order, one fact per sentence: where it happens, what goes in, what happens, what comes out. Use the exact terms (photolysis, ATP synthase, denaturation).
traps: Vague words like 'it breaks down' without saying what, where or why
Mixing up the cyclic and non-cyclic pathways, or the light-dependent and light-independent stages
Describing the steps in the wrong order
Answering 'outline' with a single sentence

questionTypes.name: Experiment design, variables and conclusions
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q2(d) (sugar and fermentation rate), Q6(a) (pH and bacterial growth), Q7(c) (light and algal beads). Sample 2 Q6 (light intensity and photosynthesis), Q7 (glucose test) and Q1(b) (vaccine trial). These sit inside the longer questions, not in a separate section.
questionTypes.see: A short description of an experiment, then items on the dependent variable, a control, a limitation or an improvement. Example, Sample 1 Q6(a)(iv): 'It can be difficult to measure the diameter of the colonies when they merge together after a period of time. Suggest one way the student could have overcome this problem.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published for the samples. Variables have exact answers, so the independent variable (what is changed) and dependent variable (what is measured) need to be named, not described loosely. A named condition and how it is kept constant scores as a pair.
questionTypes.play: Write 'independent: [the thing changed]; dependent: [the thing measured]'. For constants, name the condition (temperature) and the way you keep it constant (water bath at 25 °C). For improvements, add repeats or a bigger sample.
traps: Swapping the independent and dependent variables
Saying 'keep everything the same' without naming a factor
Naming a condition but not saying how to control it
Concluding beyond the data: for instance, a result with one species does not show all bacteria behave that way

questionTypes.name: Justify, agree or disagree, discuss
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q6(b)(iv) (is this a testable hypothesis?), Q7(a)(v) (avoid bias). Sample 2 Q2(a)(v) (agree or disagree with a statement about the species counts), Q3(a)(iii) (is a pH buffer necessary for PCR), Q3(d)(v) (discuss one ethical issue in genetic technologies).
questionTypes.see: A statement or issue, and the words 'justify', 'agree or disagree' or 'discuss'. Example, Sample 2 Q3(a)(iii): 'A student states that: "a pH buffer is not a necessary component for PCR". Do you agree or disagree with this statement? Justify your answer.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published for the samples. A position alone scores little. Expect the marks to be for the reason: a correct biological fact that supports the position you chose.
questionTypes.play: Pick a side in the first four words, then give two supporting facts. For 'discuss', give a point, its effect and a counter-point. For a testable hypothesis, say it can be tested because you could measure an outcome in a treated and an untreated group.
traps: Agreeing or disagreeing with no reason
Giving an opinion instead of a biological fact
Sitting on the fence for a 'discuss' question: say what the issue is and who it affects

questionTypes.name: Tables, matching and compare
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q2(b)(iii) (tick the characteristics of plants and fungi), Q3(c)(ii) (write High or Low for gas concentrations in blood), Q5(c)(ii) (match hormones to effects and graph letters). Sample 2 Q4(a)(iii) (distinguish bacteria and fungi), Q7 (complete a table of biomolecules).
questionTypes.see: A table where you tick, match or write one word per box. Example, Sample 1 Q2(b)(iii): 'Compare the kingdoms by placing a tick in the appropriate boxes in the table below. Note: a characteristic may be present for both kingdoms.'
questionTypes.marked: No scheme published. Each box is a separate small mark, so one error does not wipe the whole table. The paper warns that a characteristic may be present for both, so you may need two ticks on a row.
questionTypes.play: Go row by row and decide plants, fungi, both, or neither. If you are unsure of a tick, think what you know about the organism: chitin cell walls, no chloroplasts and heterotrophic feeding are fungi.
traps: Ticking only one column when the row is true for both
Writing 'high' for both blood types because the question looked easy
Mixing the match letter with the hormone name
